A pharmaceutical quality system, often called a PQS, brings
together the people, processes and management arrangements used to maintain medicine
quality. Good Manufacturing Practice is a fundamental part of this system.
A strong quality system defines responsibilities, establishes procedures, monitors performance and
supports continual improvement. It does not rely on final product testing
alone.
Senior management is accountable for establishing an effective pharmaceutical quality system
and providing suitable resources. Responsibilities and authorities should be clearly defined.
Quality units, production teams, engineering and other functions must work together,
while preserving required independent quality decisions. Management review uses information about
performance, problems and improvement opportunities to guide action.
Quality risk management provides a structured way to assess, control, communicate
and review risks to product quality. The level of formality, effort
and documentation should reflect the risk and available knowledge. Risk assessments
are not a substitute for meeting regulatory requirements. For example, the
criticality of a temperature sensor depends on its intended function and
potential effect on product quality.
When work departs from an approved procedure or expected result, the
event should be documented and evaluated through applicable quality procedures. Investigation
depth should be proportionate to the potential impact. Corrective and preventive
action, or CAPA, should address identified causes where
appropriate. Effectiveness checks help determine whether the action achieved its intended
outcome. Not every deviation requires the same investigation or C A
P A.
Changes to equipment, processes, software, facilities or documents can affect validated
status and product quality. A formal change management process evaluates proposed
changes before implementation. The assessment considers technical impact, regulatory implications, validation
needs, training and required approvals. After implementation, the organization verifies that
the change was completed as intended and that necessary evidence is
available.
Good documentation practices help ensure that instructions are clear and records
accurately describe work performed. An approved standard operating procedure explains how
to perform a defined activity. A completed record provides evidence of
what actually happened. Entries should be accurate, legible, attributable and made
at the time of the activity, according to applicable procedures. Corrections
must preserve the original information and remain traceable.
Data integrity means that information is complete, consistent and accurate throughout
its lifecycle. The ALCOA principles include attributable,
legible, contemporaneous, original and accurate. Additional expectations often described as A
L C O A plus include complete, consistent, enduring and available.
These concepts apply to both paper and electronic records. Access controls,
audit trails and record retention should be appropriate to the system
and its risks.
Consider a manufacturing vessel whose critical instrument has an expired calibration
status. The operator should not simply ignore the finding. The equipment
suitability and potential product quality impact must be assessed under approved
site procedures. The decision, rationale and any necessary corrective action should
be documented. This example connects the pharmaceutical quality system, risk management
and good documentation practices to a real operational decision.
